archetype.name: Game Manager (spot-start backup)
archetype.definition: A veteran backup who wins, when he does, by playing on schedule: quick, short throws, checkdowns to his back and few shots downfield, with no physical tools to rescue a play once it breaks down.

report.headline: Two bad cameos sent him to QB3; the film says that was earned.
report.take:
Cooper Rush is a ninth-year undrafted backup whose game has always been the same. He gets the ball out, keeps it short and lets the offense around him do the work. His career shows a quarterback who has never completed passes above expectation (CPOE negative in every season on file) and who survived on avoiding sacks and avoiding the back-breaking mistake. In 2026 the second half of that bargain fell apart. He opened the year as Atlanta's Week 1 starter, lost a winnable game at Pittsburgh, came off the bench in a 3-34 home loss to Carolina in Week 2, and has since watched Michael Penix Jr. start five straight. As of mid-October the depth chart lists him third.

The two games were not unlucky. They were bad in a way that fits who he is. His intended air yards sit at 5.34 and he threw aggressively into tight windows on just 7.69% of attempts, so the offense was running on throws at or behind the sticks. When he did push the ball past 10 yards it went badly wrong: 9 such attempts produced 3 completions, 3 interceptions and -13.2 EPA. His -0.635 EPA per dropback ranks 44th of 45 qualifiers, and his 10.3% interception rate ranks dead last. Third downs, where a game manager is supposed to earn his keep, produced a 15.4% conversion rate with an average of 8.5 yards to go. He couldn't stay ahead of the chains, and once behind them he had no answer.

The numbers hide two things worth separating. First, the sacks. A 62.5% pressure-to-sack rate is out of character for a quarterback who ranked 2nd of 62 in that stat last season and 4th in 2022. Behind a line that ranks 3rd in hit rate allowed, and on a pressure sample this small, that number should come back toward his norm. Second, the accuracy. A 23.1% bad-throw rate, up 5.8 points on last season, alongside a CPOE down 11.7 points, is a real decline layered on a quarterback whose EPA per play has dropped every season since 2021. The first is noise; the second is a trend.

Where it heads is simple. With Penix entrenched and Tua Tagovailoa also on the roster, Rush is an emergency option, not a contributor. His season line will probably stay frozen at two games. The only question that matters is how ugly it gets if injuries force him back in.

strengths.title: Short game stays near break-even
strengths.body: On throws of 0-9 air yards he was roughly neutral, with a 50% success rate and EPA a hair below zero. That is the zone his whole career is built on. It won't win games alone, but it means he can run a quick-game script without actively sinking the offense. It's sustainable because it matches his profile in every past season.

strengths.title: Career-long sack avoidance
strengths.body: Historically Rush gets rid of the ball under pressure: he ranked 2nd in pressure-to-sack rate in 2025 and 4th in 2022. This year's sack spike came on a small number of pressured dropbacks, and Atlanta's line ranks among the league's best at keeping hits off the quarterback. If he plays again, expect the sack rate to fall back toward his norm.

strengths.title: Comfortable working the left side
strengths.body: Throws to his left were his one productive area: 12 attempts, 83.3% completions and positive EPA, while the middle and right sides were disasters. His few under-center snaps (five plays) were also efficient, a hint that structured play-action suits him better than empty shotgun. Both are tiny samples, useful for how a staff might script him rather than proof of a skill.

concerns.title: Turnovers the moment he pushes downfield
concerns.body: Three of his four interceptions came on intermediate throws, and passes of 10-plus air yards cost Atlanta more EPA than everything else he did combined. This is the core flaw, not a fluke. With limited arm talent and declining accuracy, he struggles to fit throws into the 10-19 yard window, so defenses can sit on his checkdowns and dare him to throw over the top. At this rate the pace17 line projects to 34 interceptions, which is why the staff stopped playing him.

concerns.title: Accuracy slipping year over year
concerns.body: His CPOE of -13.61 ranks 44th of 45, and his bad-throw rate jumped to 23.1% from 17.3% a season ago. His EPA per play has fallen every season on file, from +0.108 in 2021 to -0.436 in 2025. At nearly 33, that looks like a skill eroding rather than a two-game slump, and it removes the margin a low-aDOT passer needs.

concerns.title: Can't convert behind the chains
concerns.body: On third down he converted 15.4% of chances, with a -36.1 CPOE and three sacks on 13 plays. Because he throws so short of the sticks by design, long third downs force him into exactly the throws he can't make. That is a structural cost of his style, made worse this year by poor accuracy.

trend.note: Week 1 at Pittsburgh was poor but competitive; Week 2 against Carolina was worse, with a 29.4% bad-throw rate and a -16.8 CPOE in relief. He hasn't taken a snap since and has slid to third on the depth chart.

nextGame.headline: Inactive or idle as QB3; Tampa's defense would smother him
nextGame.body:
Should Rush see the field at Tampa, it is close to the worst possible matchup for his style. The Buccaneers rank 2nd in pass defense EPA and 3rd against short passes, exactly where Rush lives. Tampa's weak spot is the deep ball, where it ranks 17th, but he attempted only two throws of 20-plus yards all season. Tampa has also held opposing WR1s furthest under their averages of any defense, so Drake London, the only target who produced positive EPA with Rush, would be hard to lean on.

Availability is the whole story. Penix has started Weeks 3 through 7, and Rush sat third on the depth chart as of October 19, so he only plays if two quarterbacks ahead of him go down or a blowout opens mop-up snaps. On Tampa's side, safety Antoine Winfield Jr. (97% of snaps) is out, which softens the back end, but that helps a downfield passer more than Rush. Atlanta's own absences (Zaccheaus, Brian Robinson Jr., Beaux Collins) thin depth without changing his outlook. An early forecast shows a chance of thunderstorms, too far out to matter.

keyMatchups.title: His checkdowns versus Tampa's short defense
keyMatchups.body: Rush's offense runs through throws under 10 air yards, and Tampa allows less EPA on short passes than all but two defenses. With no downfield game to loosen coverage, his already break-even short game would likely turn negative.

keyMatchups.title: London against a WR1-erasing defense
keyMatchups.body: London was Rush's only efficient target, while Bijan Robinson drew the most targets but lost EPA on them. Tampa ranks 1st in holding WR1s under their averages, which would leave Rush leaning even harder on checkdowns that already weren't working.

keyMatchups.title: Light pass rush, but it may not matter
keyMatchups.body: Tampa ranks 24th in hit rate, so Rush would likely have a clean pocket. That plays to his career habit of avoiding sacks, but his problems this year came from inaccurate throws, not pressure.

nextGame.watch: Whether Rush is active on game day and where he sits behind Penix and Tagovailoa. His snap count is the only stat that matters.

restOfSeason.body: Expect little to nothing. As QB3 behind an established starter, Rush's realistic weekly line is zero attempts, at most 0-2 in a lopsided game. If injuries do force him into a start, his career says he'd be a below-average checkdown passer rather than this year's turnover machine. The sack rate and 10%-plus interception rate should regress toward his history, which puts a spot start in the 120-190 passing-yard range with roughly one interception and a couple of sacks. What won't regress is the accuracy decline and the inability to threaten the intermediate and deep levels, which cap any start at game-manager output against a run-leaning Atlanta offense.
